ad.intro1.html: SPF says which servers may send for the domain; DMARC tells recipients what to do with mail that does not authenticate. The panel writes them on Cloudflare with the account already linked to the domain, the same one it uses for DKIM rotation. If a record of that kind already exists, it leaves it alone: it stops and shows it to you.
ad.intro2.html: The check looks at the content of the records, not the name: a google-site-verification at the apex has nothing to do with SPF and must not stop it from being created. And if there were two records, it says so: two SPF records on the same name give permerror and SPF stops working altogether (RFC 7208 §4.5), two DMARC records are both discarded (RFC 9989). These failures give no signal: mail keeps leaving, and one day it starts landing in spam.
ad.intro3.html: “Set up everything” runs the whole chain for this domain, in one click: DKIM keys and record, SPF, the report mailbox, DMARC in monitoring mode, autoconfig, the two SRV records, and then MTA-STS in full: the include line in nginx, the port 443 setup, the jail, the mta-sts CNAME, the proxy turned off on that name, a certificate covering it, the wait for propagation, the policy test and finally the TXT record. DNS, nginx and certificate do not work separately if you want MTA-STS: it is one chain, run by one sequence, the same as the “Activate MTA-STS” button, which does it for every domain instead of one. At the first step that fails it stops and explains what is missing.
ad.noReportBoxWhy: Today mail addressed to {address} goes nowhere: there is no mailbox with that name, and no forwarding sends it elsewhere. Until that changes, publishing DMARC would help little: the reports would leave and all bounce.

Turn on MTA-STS on every domain?

The panel runs, in order: the include line in nginx, the 443 configuration, the fail2ban jail, one mta-sts CNAME per domain, the Cloudflare proxy off on those names, a certificate covering them, the policy test, and finally the TXT record.

The TXT record is published ONLY for the domains whose policy really answers. At the first step that fails it stops and explains.

No record other than mta-sts is touched: a wildcard *.domain, if any, stays exactly as it is.

Where it creates or fixes a record, the sequence waits for the DNS to propagate before testing the policy: so it can take a few minutes. The work goes on on the server even if you close the page.

cfi.intro1.html: Both panels sit behind Cloudflare, so every request comes from an edge address. The real address of whoever knocks is in the CF-Connecting-IP header, and the panel trusts it only if the connection comes from an address it recognizes as Cloudflare — otherwise anyone could write whatever they like in it and forge their entry in the logs.
cfi.intro2.html: That list is written by hand inside the panel and must stay the same as the official one. If Cloudflare adds a range and starts serving from it, the panel stops recognizing it: from then on every visitor becomes a single address, and the login attempt limit applies to everyone together — five wrong attempts by anyone would lock you out too. It fails by becoming stricter, which is the quietest way to break.
cfi.intro3.html: This check only reads: it downloads the two official lists and compares them. It updates nothing by itself — a list of who deserves trust is not rewritten without a human having looked at it.

fw.port25Advice.html: Advice: leave it off. The bots knocking on port 25 usually try to use you as an open relay, but Postfix already turns them away with Relay access denied: that noise in the logs is harmless. Turning it on gains almost nothing in security and risks losing legitimate incoming mail.

fw.port25What.html: What it does: normally the country whitelist only protects the login ports (587, 465, 143, 993, 110, 995), where attackers try to guess passwords. Port 25 stays open to everyone instead: it is the port other mail servers (Gmail, Microsoft, your friends' and customers' servers) use to deliver your incoming mail.
fw.port25When.html: When to turn it on: only if you are 100% sure nobody will ever write to you from a mail server in a country outside the whitelist (for example China, India, Vietnam, Brazil). Even a small foreign supplier could send you legitimate invoices or notices.

jc.pfDdosCatches: Huge numbers of connections from the same IP in a few seconds.
jc.pfDdosMisses: Attacks spread over many different IPs.
jc.pfMoreCatches: SASL failures + improper command pipelining + basic rejects.
jc.pfMoreMisses: Probes that only connect/disconnect with auth=0/N.
jc.pfSaslCatches: Only "SASL authentication failed" (real login attempts with a wrong password).
jc.pfSaslMisses: SMTP scanners and bots that try AUTH and disconnect without an explicit SASL error.

lg.connectionsCatch: Finds: every incoming connection (to see who contacts you).

lg.errorsDesc.html: Errors and warnings of every service: the first filter to try when something is wrong and you do not know where to look.
lg.knownScannersCatch: Finds: the names of scanners known to be harmless. Useful to recognize the noise.
lg.knownScannersDesc.html: Known bots and scanners: only the hosts whose name identifies them as public security scanners. Harmless: recognize them so you do not mistake them for attacks.
lg.mailBounceCatch: Finds: rejected, bounced or deferred messages. The place to look when someone says mail does not arrive.
lg.mailBounceDesc.html: Bounced and rejected: messages NOT delivered (permanent bounces, deferred, rejected). The first place to look when someone says their mail did not arrive.
lg.mailSentDesc.html: Mail delivered: the delivered messages. If you look for a specific one, add the sender or the recipient to the filter.

lg.scannersCatch: Finds: internet scanners (Censys, Shodan, BinaryEdge and similar) probing the mail ports with malformed requests. They are NOT attacks, just internet noise.
lg.scannersDesc.html: Internet scanners: probes from public scanners (Censys, Shodan, BinaryEdge...) knocking on the mail ports with malformed requests. They are NOT attacks, just internet noise: Postfix answers that it speaks TLS and that is the end of it.
lg.spamDesc.html: Spam and viruses: anti-spam (Rspamd) and antivirus (ClamAV) events: messages marked as spam, scores, viruses found.

sj.confirmBanAction:
Fix the ban command of the panel's jails?

These jails ban with a command that does not exist on FreeBSD: they detect attacks, count bans, and block nobody.

The panel declares the pf action, copies the files before touching them, reloads fail2ban, and then asks fail2ban which command it runs, to check that the fix took. If fail2ban refuses the configuration, the files go back as they were.

It does not touch pf or the firewall rules.

Go ahead?

• The .db file is compiled again with postalias.
• Postfix is reloaded.

sj.confirmFixAll:
🪄 FIX EVERYTHING, in the right order:

1. Installs Fail2ban (if missing)
2. Enables it at boot
3. Sets up the mail-panel-auth jail
4. Sets up the Postfix, Dovecot, Roundcube and Rspamd jails
5. Creates a minimal /etc/pf.conf (if missing)
6. Adds the f2b anchor to pf.conf
7. Enables pf at boot
8. Starts pf (with a syntax check first)
9. Starts Fail2ban

⚠️ It touches pf too (the firewall): with an unusual custom pf.conf there is a theoretical risk of being locked out, but the panel makes a backup copy and checks the syntax before applying.

Physical or console access to the server is recommended.

Go ahead?

sj.confirmPf:
WARNING: operation on pf (the system firewall)

You are about to change or start the server firewall.

RISK: a wrong pf configuration can lock you out of the server completely, SSH and this panel INCLUDED.

The panel checks the syntax and makes a backup copy, but the risk is NOT zero.

Before confirming, make sure you have physical or console access to the server (KVM, IPMI, serial console) to recover if something goes wrong.

Go ahead?

Reload fail2ban?

It reads the configuration files again without stopping the daemon. The counters and the current bans stay.
sj.confirmRestart:
⚠️ RESTART of fail2ban (service fail2ban restart)

It stops the daemon and starts it from scratch. Useful to get out of confused states (for example after many reloads).

WHAT HAPPENS:
• The "failed now" and "failed in total" counters are RESET
• The current bans are LOST (but the permanent pf bans stay)
• The configuration in jail.local is READ again from scratch
• A few seconds without monitoring

sts.intro1.html: Between two mail servers TLS is opportunistic: if the recipient does not offer STARTTLS, the message leaves anyway, in clear text. An attacker in the middle can strip that offer as it passes, and the sender has no way to notice. MTA-STS closes that door: it declares in advance that your servers always have TLS, and that whoever cannot manage it must not deliver.
sts.intro2.html: It takes three pieces together, which is why the record is not created by itself: an mta-sts CNAME, the policy served over HTTPS on that name with a certificate valid for that name, and only at the end the TXT record that declares it. The TXT is not published until the policy really answers: it would be a public promise you do not keep.

At the first step that fails they stop and explain what is missing. The button above is only for publishing the TXT of a single domain by hand.

up.releaseIntro.html:
What the panel does. The preliminary checks, the copy of /etc, the way back (a ZFS boot environment you return to with one command), the pending patches, then freebsd-update install repeated as many times as needed — reading what freebsd-update asks for and acting on it — the reboots, and the final check against the inventory taken before. It remembers where it is, so it survives the reboots.
What is left to you, and only that: the first command, freebsd-update -r <version> upgrade. Not for the confirmation it asks — that would be trivial — but because it may open an editor to merge the files in /etc: they include master.passwd, rc.conf and the Postfix files, and a merge decided by automation is the way to break something without anyone noticing. It rarely happens, but when it does it takes a person.

up.sorvIntro1.html: The rules this panel is built on change, and until now we noticed by chance, while doing something else. On 1 September 2026 it happened with DMARC: the panel was written on RFC 7489, replaced in May by three new documents, and nobody had said so.
up.sorvIntro2.html: That discovery could be automated: the RFC Editor publishes the state of every document in a machine-readable form. The panel queries it for each specification it implements and says whether it has been replaced or updated. The same items go into the periodic report, so they arrive by email instead of waiting for someone to come by here.

up.w443Intro1.html: Two features need port 443 because the protocols allow no other port: the MTA-STS policy, read by sending servers all over the world, and the Thunderbird configuration file. Opening that port exposes something, so that something must be as little as possible.
up.w443Intro2.html: The block the panel installs is separate from the webmail one on 8443 — if it were added inside it, it would inherit Roundcube's root and the PHP handler, opening a whole application to serve two text files. It has default_server, so no other site can answer on that port; only two exact location blocks and 404 for everything else; only GET and HEAD; rate and connection limits per address; short timeouts. The MTA-STS policy is a static file: a request there never reaches the panel or the database.
up.webIntro1.html: The panel contains two install scripts that write different nginx configurations: one puts a block on port 80 that serves the webmail in clear text, the other only the encrypted 443. Looking at the code you cannot tell which one built this machine.
up.webIntro2.html: This diagnosis reads nginx -T, the full configuration as nginx really sees it, plus the listening ports, the pf rules and the fail2ban jails. It changes nothing. And if a command fails it says so, instead of concluding that all is well.

w4.confirmInclude:
Add the include line to the main nginx configuration?

It is inserted at the top of the http block, with a backup. Then nginx -t: if it fails, the previous file is put back and nothing is reloaded.
w4.confirmInstall:
Install the public configuration on port 443?

It serves TWO files and nothing else: the MTA-STS policy and the Thunderbird configuration. Every other path gets 404.

The panel makes a copy, runs nginx -t and only then reloads. If validation fails it removes everything without reloading: the webmail on 8443 is not touched.
w4.confirmJail:
Enable the fail2ban jail for port 443?

It bans for one hour whoever collects ten 404, 405 or 429 answers in ten minutes. It looks only at this site's log, not the webmail one.
